episode_title: Episode 174: Beyond Disordered Eating: Rebuilding Your Relationship with Food (Part 2)

real_qa.q: What is orthorexia and why does it remain hidden in the wellness space?
real_qa.r: Orthorexia is a proposed mental health condition where healthy eating becomes obsessive, rigid, and fear-based, negatively affecting wellbeing. It appears hidden in wellness spaces because it manifests as extreme clean eating, biohacking, organic-only consumption, and constant searching for the perfect diet—behaviors often praised as health-conscious rather than recognized as disordered. The condition shows up when someone experiences panic and shame around eating foods outside their prescribed way, substantially affecting their life.

real_qa.q: How does perfectionism drive disordered eating patterns?
real_qa.r: Perfectionism operates as a control pattern and safety mechanism where people believe eating a certain way or consuming specific calorie amounts will ensure everything is okay. It typically stems from early patterns of high achievement and discipline used to gain approval and protect from criticism. When emotions were not welcomed in childhood but achievement was praised, perfectionism becomes tied to identity and self-worth, manifesting through food and body control as a way to maintain that approval and love.

real_qa.q: What is the connection between chronic stress, the nervous system, and gut barrier dysfunction?
real_qa.r: Digestion is supported by the parasympathetic nervous system in the rest-and-digest state, but during stress the blood flow is shunted away from digestive organs to survival organs. Chronic or repeated stress activates the brain's CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone), which communicates with the gut and activates mast cells that release histamine and inflammatory cytokines. These compounds affect tight junctions in the gut lining, making the barrier more permeable, allowing bacterial fragments and food antigens to interact with the immune system and cause inflammation, creating a feedback loop.
real_qa.requete: stress gut barrier tight junctions CRH mast cells

real_qa.q: How does stress and anxiety around food specifically impact digestive function in women with disordered eating?
real_qa.r: Even imagined threats trigger the same physiological stress response as real threats—so worrying about what you are eating or feeling guilty about food causes the same nervous system changes. This diverts blood flow away from the digestive system needed to digest food, affecting stomach acid, enzymes, and bile flow, causing bloating and changes in bowel movements. Additionally, chronic stress increases gut sensitivity and makes the gut barrier more permeable through the stress-activated pathways, creating a cycle where disordered eating behavior itself perpetuates gut dysfunction.
real_qa.requete: stress anxiety food digestion women nervous system

real_qa.q: How can food and body control become a mask for deeper emotional needs in women?
real_qa.r: Women often use food and body control to meet unmet emotional needs such as feeling acceptable, safer, more desirable, less judged, or more in control. However, this strategy fails long-term because the body is always changing—through the menstrual cycle, postpartum, and with aging. If someone only feels okay when their body looks a certain way, they will experience feelings of being unsafe every time the body changes, leading to escalating and unsustainable control goals. The deeper work is learning to make health choices through self-compassion rather than self-hatred.
real_qa.requete: food body control emotional needs women

real_qa.q: Why do clients with disordered eating behaviors often confuse volume and food density with actual food intolerances?
real_qa.r: When someone has become controlling about food portions and has restricted to smaller amounts, consuming more food feels physically heavier in the digestive tract. This heaviness can be misinterpreted as a food problem or intolerance when it is actually about the volume and density change. Additionally, the brain rationalizes this sensation as proof the food is bad for them, reinforcing restrictive patterns. This misattribution is compounded when clients are out of sync with their natural hunger and fullness cues.
real_qa.requete: food volume density intolerance disordered eating

She brings both clinical knowledge and lived experience to her work with clients navigating food anxiety and body control issues.
